standard.title: Evaluate solutions against design criteria
standard.description: discuss how existing and student solutions satisfy the design criteria and user stories
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can discuss how existing digital systems satisfy identified needs for known users (AC9TDI2P03). They have discussed fit-for-purpose at a general level. They have not yet evaluated solutions explicitly against design criteria and user stories as structured evaluation tools.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students discuss how both existing digital solutions and their own student-created solutions satisfy specific design criteria and user stories, giving reasons grounded in the criteria.

nodes.label: Describing what a solution does for users
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe what an existing digital solution does and who it helps
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one existing digital solution and explain what task it helps users complete
nodes.typical_width: Describe how familiar digital solutions (maps, online orders, interactive directories) allow users to complete specific tasks; identify who benefits and what need each solution addresses
wider: Investigate how a digital solution used in a First Nations community context (e.g. GPS tools for ranger land management) helps specific users — describe what the tool does and who it helps in that context
Describe how library management systems help different users (librarians tracking loans, students finding books) — discuss how the same solution serves different user needs simultaneously
success_criteria: Names at least one task the solution helps users complete
Identifies the user group the solution is designed for
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot describe what a solution does for users cannot perform criteria evaluation in N2 — evaluation requires knowing what the solution actually does before checking it against criteria.

nodes.label: Evaluating against design criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can check a solution against specific design criteria and state whether each criterion is met with a reason
nodes.minimum_width: Given a solution and one or two criteria, state whether each criterion is met and give one reason
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate an existing or student solution against a set of design criteria; for each criterion, state whether it is met and provide a reason; identify criteria the solution meets well and criteria it partially or does not meet
wider: Evaluate a digital solution against criteria that include accessibility or equity considerations — for example, a solution that works well for urban users but fails for users in areas with limited connectivity
Evaluate a student-created game against criteria from both the designer's and a classmate's perspective — discuss how the same solution can be judged differently depending on who is evaluating

response_modes.reason: Evaluation against criteria requires students to make a criterion-by-criterion judgement move rather than a general impression. Scaffolding the process (identify the criterion → check the solution against it → state whether it is met → give a reason) prevents students from evaluating by opinion alone.

success_criteria: States clearly whether a criterion is met
Gives a reason that references a specific feature of the solution, not just a general impression
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who evaluate by general impression rather than criterion-by-criterion reasoning cannot engage with N3's user story evaluation — both require the same structured judgement move applied to different frameworks.

nodes.label: Evaluating against user stories
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can check a solution against a user story and discuss how well it meets the user's need and purpose
nodes.minimum_width: Given a solution and one user story, discuss whether the solution meets the user's need and purpose
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate existing and student solutions against user stories for different contexts; discuss how well the solution meets both the need and the purpose (the 'so that' part) of the user story; identify gaps between what was designed and what was needed
wider: Evaluate a solution from the perspective of a user story you did not write — for example, evaluate a classmate's game against their user story and discuss whether the solution meets needs you might not have anticipated
Discuss a case where a solution meets the stated need but not the underlying purpose — for example, a tool that works technically but is too complex for the actual user to use

response_modes.reason: Students commonly evaluate whether the need is met but overlook the 'so that' purpose. Evaluating across different user stories — especially others' user stories — builds the habit of checking both what a solution does and whether it achieves the intended outcome.

This node integrates the design criteria evaluation from node 2 with user story evaluation — applying both simultaneously to assess a solution from multiple lenses. The integration is the learning: criteria and user stories together give a more complete evaluation than either alone.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Evaluating solutions where the stated need and underlying purpose diverge — or where different users interpret the same solution differently — is rich, generative territory. Students encounter the genuine complexity of design evaluation that goes well beyond 'does it work?'
success_criteria: References both the user's need and purpose when evaluating
Identifies at least one thing the solution does well and one gap or limitation
